name: Ultramontanism
summary: Ultramontanism is the strong emphasis on papal authority and centralization in the Catholic Church, set against Gallicanism and state control of the church and, in the nineteenth century, against liberalism and the secular state. Its key text is Pius IX's Syllabus of Errors, which condemns the separation of church and state, secular schooling, civil marriage and divorce, religious equality and the popular-sovereignty theories, and it triumphed with papal primacy and infallibility at Vatican I (1870). It is a church-political doctrine with no economic programme.
scope: Ultramontanism as the defining sources use the word: the strong emphasis on papal authority and centralization of the Roman Catholic Church (Britannica), set against Gallicanism, Febronianism, Josephinism and state control of the church, and in the nineteenth century against liberalism, laicism and the revolutionary state (Catholic Encyclopedia, Benigni 1912). Its strand is the one that triumphed at the First Vatican Council in 1870 with the definition of papal primacy and infallibility; its figures are Louis Veuillot, William George Ward, Henry Edward Manning and Pius IX, and its text the Syllabus of Errors (1864). It does not cover later Catholic social teaching, post-Vatican II views, or the 'new ultramontanism' of present-day commentators.

notes: Ultramontanism is a church-political movement; its defining sources (Britannica, the 1912 Catholic Encyclopedia, National Catholic Reporter, Church Life Journal, Britannica on Veuillot) and key work (the Syllabus of Errors) speak to church authority, church-state relations, religion, marriage, education and revolution. Searched for economy, class, nation and territory positions in all of them and found none beyond the Syllabus's condemnation of socialism and communism, so those statements are null.
